title: How does virtual-thread pinning happen (blocking I/O inside a `synchronized` block pins the carrier thread), and why replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` in virtual-thread-heavy code?
shortTitle: How does virtual-thread pinning happen, and why replace synchronized with ReentrantLock in virtual-thread-heavy code?

s1_definition.profdef: A virtual thread is a lightweight thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of platform carrier threads; when a virtual thread blocks on I/O it normally unmounts from its carrier so the carrier can run other virtual threads. Pinning is when a virtual thread cannot unmount and stays stuck to its carrier, which happens classically when it blocks inside a `synchronized` block or method, because the monitor is tied to the carrier thread. While pinned, that carrier is consumed and cannot serve other virtual threads, reducing the scalability benefit. Replacing `synchronized` with a `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` avoids pinning, because the lock is implemented in a way that lets the virtual thread unmount while it waits and while it holds the lock across a blocking call.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India having a few senior managers (carrier threads) and thousands of tasks (virtual threads). Normally, when a task has to wait on hold for an external call, it steps aside and frees the manager to help another task. Pinning is like a task that, while holding a specific office key that only works when the original manager is present (synchronized monitor), gets stuck on a long phone call; because the key is bound to that manager, the manager cannot leave to help anyone else and is wasted for the whole call. Switching to a ticket-based lock (ReentrantLock) lets the task keep its place in line without chaining a manager to its desk, so the manager is free to help others while the task waits.
s1_definition.oneliner: Virtual threads unmount from carriers when they block, but blocking inside synchronized pins them to the carrier and wastes it, so in virtual-thread-heavy code you replace synchronized with ReentrantLock to let the thread unmount.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A virtual thread is a lightweight thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of platform carrier threads; when a virtual thread blocks on I/O it normally unmounts from its carrier so the carrier can run other virtual threads. Pinning is when a virtual thread cannot unmount and stays stuck to its carrier, which happens classically when it blocks inside a `synchronized` block or method, because the monitor is tied to the carrier thread. While pinned, that carrier is consumed and cannot serve other virtual threads, reducing the scalability benefit. Replacing `synchronized` with a `java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock` avoids pinning, because the lock is implemented in a way that lets the virtual thread unmount while it waits and while it holds the lock across a blocking call.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India having a few senior managers (carrier threads) and thousands of tasks (virtual threads). Normally, when a task has to wait on hold for an external call, it steps aside and frees the manager to help another task. Pinning is like a task that, while holding a specific office key that only works when the original manager is present (synchronized monitor), gets stuck on a long phone call; because the key is bound to that manager, the manager cannot leave to help anyone else and is wasted for the whole call. Switching to a ticket-based lock (ReentrantLock) lets the task keep its place in line without chaining a manager to its desk, so the manager is free to help others while the task waits.

**One line to remember:** Virtual threads unmount from carriers when they block, but blocking inside synchronized pins them to the carrier and wastes it, so in virtual-thread-heavy code you replace synchronized with ReentrantLock to let the thread unmount.

sections.s2_technical:
Virtual threads give you millions of cheap threads because the JVM mounts a virtual thread onto a platform carrier thread only while it is running, and when it hits a blocking operation like socket I/O, the runtime unmounts it, parks the continuation, and lets the carrier pick up another virtual thread. The carrier pool is small, typically sized to the number of CPU cores, so this unmount-on-block behavior is what lets a handful of carriers serve a huge number of concurrent virtual threads. The whole model depends on virtual threads yielding their carrier whenever they wait.

Pinning breaks that. The JVM pins a virtual thread to its carrier in specific situations, the most important being when the thread is inside a synchronized block or method and then performs a blocking operation, and also when it is executing a native method or foreign function call. The reason for the synchronized case is that the object monitor's ownership is recorded against the carrier platform thread, so the runtime cannot cleanly move the virtual thread off that carrier while it owns the monitor. So if a virtual thread enters a synchronized block and then does a blocking database or network call inside it, it cannot unmount; it holds the carrier hostage for the entire duration of that blocking call. With many virtual threads doing this at once, you can exhaust the small carrier pool and your supposedly massively concurrent service grinds, because there are no free carriers left.

The fix in virtual-thread-heavy code is to replace synchronized with a ReentrantLock from the concurrency library around any critical section that contains a blocking call. A ReentrantLock's waiting and ownership are managed in Java-level data structures rather than bound to the carrier's monitor, so a virtual thread can unmount while blocked on lock acquisition and, crucially, can unmount during a blocking call made while holding the lock, freeing the carrier. For example instead of `synchronized (ledger) { balance = db.load(); }` you write `lock.lock(); try { balance = db.load(); } finally { lock.unlock(); }`, and the virtual thread no longer pins. You can detect pinning with the JDK Flight Recorder jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event or by running with the diagnostic that reports pinned stacks. A senior nuance: the strong advice is to keep critical sections small and ideally do no blocking I/O while holding any lock at all, because even with ReentrantLock, holding a lock across slow I/O serializes your throughput; also, a key practical detail is that recent JDK work has been reducing when synchronized pins, but the safe, portable guidance for high-scale virtual-thread code remains to prefer ReentrantLock and to avoid blocking inside synchronized, and never to pool virtual threads, because they are cheap and meant to be created per task.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India moved its transfer endpoint to virtual threads expecting huge concurrency, but under load throughput collapsed. The culprit was a synchronized block around the ledger update that also made a blocking database call inside it, pinning each virtual thread to its carrier for the whole call and exhausting the tiny carrier pool. This is exactly virtual-thread pinning via synchronized plus blocking I/O.

Problem 2 — The bank still needs mutual exclusion on the ledger, so it cannot just delete the lock. This is exactly what ReentrantLock solves — it provides the same mutual exclusion but lets the virtual thread unmount while it waits and while it blocks, keeping the carriers free.

The demo shows a pinning version with synchronized around a simulated blocking call and a fixed version using ReentrantLock, running many virtual threads to contrast carrier behavior, and notes how to detect pinning. Classes and steps: `PinningLedger` (synchronized, pins), `NonPinningLedger` (ReentrantLock, no pin), and `PinningDemo`.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
vthread-pinning/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   └── main/
│       └── java/com/bank/vthreads/
│           ├── PinningLedger.java            (synchronized + blocking call → pins)

```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build with Java 21+ (virtual threads are standard)
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run and compare: ReentrantLock version frees carriers and finishes faster under load
java -cp target/classes com.bank.vthreads.PinningDemo

# DETECT pinning with JDK Flight Recorder: capture jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=pin.jfr,settings=profile \
  -cp target/classes com.bank.vthreads.PinningDemo
jfr print --events jdk.VirtualThreadPinned pin.jfr   # shows the pinned stack traces

# Older JDKs also accepted -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full to print pinned stacks.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five hundred debit tasks run on virtual threads, first against the synchronized ledger, then against the ReentrantLock ledger.

Step 1 — Each task is submitted to a virtual-thread-per-task executor, so five hundred virtual threads are created cheaply, far more than the handful of carrier threads sized to the CPU cores.

Step 2 — In the synchronized version, a virtual thread enters the synchronized debit, then performs the simulated blocking database call inside the monitor. Because the monitor is bound to the carrier, the virtual thread cannot unmount, so it pins its carrier for the full fifty milliseconds, and with only a few carriers the other virtual threads queue waiting for a free carrier, so throughput collapses.

Step 3 — In the ReentrantLock version, a virtual thread acquires the lock and makes the same blocking call, but because the lock is managed in Java data structures rather than the carrier's monitor, the virtual thread unmounts during the block and frees its carrier to run another virtual thread, so the small carrier pool stays busy with useful work.

Step 4 — The timing shows the ReentrantLock version completing the five hundred debits noticeably faster under this blocking load, and both ledgers end with the correct balance because mutual exclusion is preserved; a Flight Recorder capture of the synchronized run shows jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events pointing at the synchronized debit method.

```
2026-10-26 16:20:03 [WARNING] synchronized (PINS): 6400ms, balance=Rs.999500
2026-10-26 16:20:04 [INFO] ReentrantLock (NO PIN): 850ms, balance=Rs.999500
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  500 virtual threads  ──scheduled onto──►  small carrier pool (≈ CPU cores)

  SYNCHRONIZED (pins)
    vthread → enter synchronized debit()  [monitor bound to carrier]
       │ blocking DB call INSIDE monitor
       └─ CANNOT unmount → carrier HELD for 50ms each
       → few carriers, 500 waiters → throughput collapses (6400ms)

  REENTRANTLOCK (no pin)
    vthread → lock.lock()  [lock state in Java objects, not carrier monitor]
       │ blocking DB call while holding lock
       └─ virtual thread UNMOUNTS → carrier freed to run another vthread
       → carriers stay busy with useful work (850ms)

  Detect: JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned → stack shows the synchronized method
```

                                      │ critical section guards the ledger
                                      ▼

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Pinning vs Non-Pinning Critical Section ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Lock object (ReentrantLock) instead of intrinsic monitor       │
  │    WHY: lock state in Java → virtual thread can unmount         │
  │ Thread-per-task (no pooling of virtual threads)                │
  │    WHY: virtual threads are cheap; pooling defeats the model    │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: ledger guards balance; executor manages concurrency         │
  │ D: debit() depends on a Lock abstraction, not a monitor        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Pinning Causes (as prose) ─────────────────────────────────
  blocking I/O inside synchronized : PINS (monitor bound to carrier)
  native method / FFI call          : PINS
  ReentrantLock + blocking          : does NOT pin (unmounts)
  best practice                     : no blocking I/O while holding ANY lock

  ── State: Virtual Thread on a Carrier ────────────────────────
  [MOUNTED running] ──blocking I/O (no monitor)──→ [UNMOUNTED parked] → carrier free
        │ blocking I/O INSIDE synchronized
        ▼
  [PINNED] carrier held for whole blocking call → scalability lost

  ── Call Chain (fixed) ────────────────────────────────────────
  1. vexec.submit(debit) × 500  (one vthread each)
  2.   → lock.lock()  (may unmount while waiting)
  3.   → blocking DB call  (vthread unmounts, carrier freed)
  4.   → balance -= amount ; finally lock.unlock()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Virtual threads give massive concurrency because the JVM mounts a virtual thread onto one of a small pool of platform carrier threads only while it is actually running, and when the virtual thread hits a blocking operation like socket I/O, the runtime unmounts it and lets the carrier pick up another virtual thread. The whole model depends on virtual threads yielding their carrier whenever they wait, which is how a handful of carriers can serve millions of virtual threads.

Pinning is when a virtual thread cannot unmount and stays stuck to its carrier. The classic cause is blocking inside a synchronized block or method, because the object monitor's ownership is recorded against the carrier platform thread, so the runtime cannot move the virtual thread off that carrier while it owns the monitor. So if a virtual thread enters a synchronized block and then makes a blocking database or network call inside it, it holds that carrier hostage for the entire call. When many virtual threads do this at once, they exhaust the small carrier pool and the supposedly massively concurrent service grinds to a halt because no carriers are free.

The fix in virtual-thread-heavy code is to replace synchronized with a ReentrantLock around any critical section that contains a blocking call. A ReentrantLock keeps its waiting and ownership state in ordinary Java data structures rather than in the carrier's intrinsic monitor, so a virtual thread can unmount while it waits to acquire the lock and, crucially, can unmount during a blocking call made while holding the lock, which keeps the carrier free for other work. Mutual exclusion is preserved, so I am not sacrificing correctness.

In my banking work at National Bank of India this was a real production incident. We moved the transfer endpoint to virtual threads expecting huge concurrency, but throughput collapsed under load, and a Flight Recorder capture of the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event pointed straight at a synchronized ledger method that made a blocking database call inside the monitor. We replaced the synchronized block with a ReentrantLock and the carriers stopped pinning, restoring the expected scalability. The senior points I always add are to keep critical sections tiny and ideally do no blocking I/O while holding any lock at all, because even a ReentrantLock held across slow I/O serializes throughput; to detect pinning with the Flight Recorder pinned-thread event; to never pool virtual threads because they are cheap and meant to be created one per task; and that while recent JDK work is reducing when synchronized pins, the safe, portable guidance for high-scale code remains to prefer ReentrantLock and avoid blocking inside synchronized.
